title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning

# Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning ##### 800 examples, twelve minutes, 94% accuracy A legal-tech startup needed to classify contract clauses into eleven categories. Their annotated dataset was 800 examples — nowhere near enough to train a language model from scratch, which needs billions of tokens. They fine-tuned DistilBERT instead. Twelve minutes on a single GPU, and 94% accuracy. For comparison, a colleague trained an LSTM from scratch on the same 800 examples. It reached 61% and overfit badly after four epochs. The difference is that DistilBERT already **knew English** — grammar, semantics, the fact that "indemnify" and "hold harmless" are related — from pretraining on billions of words. The 800 examples only had to teach it which of eleven buckets a clause belongs in. That is transfer learning, and it is why applied deep learning is accessible to teams without enormous datasets. ##### Why transfer learning works Yosinski et al. (2014) established the empirical finding that underpins this: **features learned by early layers are general, and features learned by late layers are specific.** In a vision model, layer 1 detects edges — useful for any image task whatsoever. Layer 5 detects textures. Layer 12 detects "golden retriever." The early representations transfer to medical imaging, satellite photos or manufacturing defects; only the final layers need replacing. The same holds in language. Early transformer layers encode syntax and part-of-speech; middle layers encode semantics; late layers encode task-specific patterns. A model pretrained on the internet has already solved "understand English," which is the expensive part. The practical consequence: **you almost never train from scratch.** You start from a checkpoint someone spent millions of dollars producing and adapt it for the cost of a coffee. ##### Feature extraction versus fine-tuning Two strategies, and choosing between them is today's assignment. **Feature extraction** freezes the pretrained model entirely and trains only a new head on top. The pretrained weights act as a fixed feature generator. **Fine-tuning** updates the pretrained weights too, usually with a much smaller learning rate, so the representations adapt to your domain. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn from transformers import AutoModel, AutoModelForSequenceClassification # --- Feature extraction: freeze the backbone --- model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained( "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=11) for param in model.distilbert.parameters(): param.requires_grad = False # backbone frozen trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) print(f"Training {trainable:,} of {total:,} parameters ({trainable/total:.1%})") # Training 8,459 of 66,371,339 parameters (0.0%) # --- Fine-tuning: everything trainable --- model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained( "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=11) # all parameters trainable by default ``` The decision hinges primarily on **dataset size**: | Your data | Similarity to pretraining domain | Strategy | |---|---|---| | Small (<1,000) | Similar | **Feature extraction** — too little data to fine-tune safely | | Small (<1,000) | Different | Fine-tune the top few layers only | | Medium (1k–10k) | Similar | Fine-tune the top half | | Medium (1k–10k) | Different | **Full fine-tuning** with a low learning rate | | Large (>10k) | Either | **Full fine-tuning** | The reasoning: fine-tuning 66 million parameters on 300 examples will overfit catastrophically — there is not enough signal to constrain that many weights. Feature extraction trains only a few thousand parameters, which 300 examples can support. The other axis is cost. Feature extraction is fast, needs little memory, and lets you precompute embeddings once and reuse them. Full fine-tuning typically yields several points more accuracy when you have the data. ##### Fine-tuning a transformer ```python from transformers import (AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer, DataCollatorWithPadding, EarlyStoppingCallback) from datasets import Dataset import numpy as np from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score MODEL = "distilbert-base-uncased" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL) labels = ["indemnity", "termination", "confidentiality", ...] model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained( MODEL, num_labels=len(labels), id2label={i: l for i, l in enumerate(labels)}, # saved with the model label2id={l: i for i, l in enumerate(labels)}, ) def tokenize(batch): return tokenizer(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=256) train_ds = Dataset.from_dict({"text": train_texts, "label": train_labels}).map( tokenize, batched=True, remove_columns=["text"]) val_ds = Dataset.from_dict({"text": val_texts, "label": val_labels}).map( tokenize, batched=True, remove_columns=["text"]) def compute_metrics(eval_pred): logits, y_true = eval_pred y_pred = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1) return { "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), "f1_macro": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average="macro"), } args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./results", learning_rate=2e-5, # SMALL — see below per_device_train_batch_size=16, per_device_eval_batch_size=64, num_train_epochs=4, # 2-4 is typical; more overfits weight_decay=0.01, warmup_ratio=0.1, # gradual LR ramp-up lr_scheduler_type="linear", eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="f1_macro", fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(), # mixed precision: ~2x faster logging_steps=50, seed=42, ) trainer = Trainer( model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds, eval_dataset=val_ds, tokenizer=tokenizer, data_collator=DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer), # dynamic padding per batch compute_metrics=compute_metrics, callbacks=[EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=2)], ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model("./contract-classifier") tokenizer.save_pretrained("./contract-classifier") ``` Three settings do most of the work. **`learning_rate=2e-5`** — roughly 50× smaller than you would use training from scratch. This is the single most important hyperparameter in fine-tuning. Too high and you destroy the pretrained knowledge in the first few steps; the useful range is 1e-5 to 5e-5 for transformers. **`num_train_epochs=4`** — fine-tuning converges fast. Two to four epochs is standard; ten will overfit almost any small dataset. **`DataCollatorWithPadding`** pads each batch to its own longest sequence rather than a global maximum, which is meaningfully faster when sequence lengths vary. Note also `id2label` and `label2id` in the model config. They travel with the saved model, so at inference time the pipeline returns `"indemnity"` rather than `LABEL_3`. ##### Fine-tuning a CNN The same pattern in vision, with explicit layer freezing: ```python import torchvision.models as models model = models.resnet50(weights=models.ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2) # 1. Freeze everything for param in model.parameters(): param.requires_grad = False # 2. Replace the classifier head — new layers are trainable by default model.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, num_classes), ) # 3. Optionally unfreeze the last convolutional block for param in model.layer4.parameters(): param.requires_grad = True # 4. Discriminative learning rates — lower for pretrained, higher for new optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW([ {"params": model.layer4.parameters(), "lr": 1e-4}, # pretrained: gentle {"params": model.fc.parameters(), "lr": 1e-3}, # new head: faster ], weight_decay=1e-4) ``` **Discriminative learning rates** are worth adopting generally: pretrained layers already hold useful weights and need only small adjustments, while the randomly-initialized head needs to learn from nothing. Applying one rate to both either destroys the backbone or starves the head. The other essential vision detail is **matching the pretraining preprocessing**. A model trained on ImageNet expects ImageNet's normalization statistics: ```python from torchvision import transforms transform = transforms.Compose([ transforms.Resize(256), transforms.CenterCrop(224), transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], # ImageNet statistics std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]), ]) ``` Using different normalization shifts the input distribution away from what every pretrained layer expects, and accuracy drops noticeably for no visible reason. ##### Progressive unfreezing A refinement that often outperforms both pure strategies: train the head first with everything frozen, then unfreeze progressively. ```python def progressive_unfreeze(model, train_fn, stages): """Train the head, then unfreeze deeper layers stage by stage.""" for param in model.parameters(): param.requires_grad = False for param in model.classifier.parameters(): param.requires_grad = True for stage, (layers_to_unfreeze, lr, epochs) in enumerate(stages, 1): for layer in layers_to_unfreeze: for param in layer.parameters(): param.requires_grad = True optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW( filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, model.parameters()), lr=lr) print(f"Stage {stage}: lr={lr}, " f"trainable={sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad):,}") train_fn(model, optimizer, epochs) ``` The rationale is about gradient quality. A randomly-initialized head produces large, noisy gradients in the first epochs. If the backbone is unfrozen at that point, those noisy gradients flow into carefully-pretrained weights and damage them. Training the head first lets it stabilize, after which the gradients reaching the backbone are informative rather than destructive. ##### Catastrophic forgetting **Catastrophic forgetting** is the loss of pretrained knowledge during fine-tuning — the model becomes excellent at your 800 contracts and noticeably worse at general English. The symptom is subtle: strong performance on your task, poor performance on anything slightly outside your training distribution. A sentiment model fine-tuned only on movie reviews may fail on product reviews it would have handled before fine-tuning. Five mitigations: **Low learning rate.** 2e-5 rather than 1e-3. The most important single defence. **Few epochs** with early stopping — every additional epoch drifts further from the pretrained weights. **Freeze early layers**, which hold the most general knowledge. **Discriminative learning rates**, so deeper layers change less. **Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA)** — freeze the original weights entirely and train small low-rank adapter matrices instead: ```python from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType config = LoraConfig( task_type=TaskType.SEQ_CLS, r=8, # rank of the adapter matrices lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0.1, target_modules=["q_lin", "v_lin"], # attention query and value projections ) model = get_peft_model(base_model, config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable params: 739,586 || all params: 67,110,925 || trainable%: 1.10 ``` LoRA trains roughly 1% of the parameters, produces adapter files of a few megabytes rather than gigabytes, is much harder to overfit on small data, and **cannot cause catastrophic forgetting because the original weights never change.** For large models it is now the default approach. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Task + dataset] --> B{How much labelled data?} B -->|under 1k| C[FEATURE EXTRACTION
freeze backbone, train head] B -->|1k to 10k| D{Domain similar to
pretraining?} B -->|over 10k| E[FULL FINE-TUNING
lr 2e-5, 2-4 epochs] D -->|yes| F[Fine-tune top layers
discriminative LRs] D -->|no| E C --> G[Evaluate on held-out set] F --> G E --> G G -->|overfitting| H[Lower LR, fewer epochs,
freeze more, or use LoRA] G -->|underfitting| I[Unfreeze more layers,
train longer] H --> G I --> G ``` ##### Comparing against training from scratch The comparison in today's mini project is worth running properly: ```python results = {} # 1. From scratch — same architecture, random weights from transformers import AutoConfig config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(MODEL, num_labels=len(labels)) scratch = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_config(config) # 2. Feature extraction # 3. Full fine-tuning # Typical outcome on ~1,000 examples: # from scratch: 0.42 F1 (30 epochs, still climbing slowly) # feature extraction: 0.81 F1 (5 epochs, 2 minutes) # full fine-tuning: 0.91 F1 (3 epochs, 8 minutes) ``` The gap between scratch and fine-tuned is not a matter of tuning. It reflects the billions of tokens of language knowledge the pretrained model brings and the random-weight model does not have. ##### Common mistakes - **Learning rate too high** — 1e-3 destroys pretrained weights in the first few steps. - **Too many epochs.** Fine-tuning converges in 2–4; ten overfits. - **Full fine-tuning on tiny datasets** where feature extraction is correct. - **Different preprocessing** from pretraining — wrong image normalization or a mismatched tokenizer. - **Forgetting to freeze**, then wondering why a small dataset overfits immediately. - **No `id2label` mapping**, so the deployed model outputs `LABEL_2`. - **Unfreezing everything at once** with a randomly-initialized head, corrupting the backbone. - **Skipping the from-scratch baseline**, so you cannot quantify what transfer learning bought. - **Ignoring class imbalance** — use class weights or a weighted loss. - **Not saving the tokenizer** alongside the model, making the checkpoint unusable. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **fine-tune DistilBERT on a custom text classification dataset using the Hugging Face `Trainer`**. Keep the dataset small — a thousand examples is plenty — because the point is to experience how little data and time modern fine-tuning requires. Watch the validation F1 across epochs; you will typically see it peak at epoch 2 or 3 and then decline, which is overfitting made visible. The mini project is the comparison: **fine-tune a pretrained model for a domain-specific task and compare against training from scratch**. Run all three configurations — scratch, feature extraction, full fine-tuning — on identical data with identical evaluation. Report accuracy, training time and trainable parameter count in one table. That table is the clearest evidence you can produce that transfer learning is not an optimization but a different category of approach. For the assignment, **explain feature extraction versus full fine-tuning and when to choose each based on data size**. Ground it in the parameter-to-example ratio: fine-tuning 66 million parameters with 300 labelled examples has no chance of being constrained by the data, whereas training an 8,000-parameter head does. Then add the second axis — domain similarity — and note that LoRA now offers a middle path, training around 1% of parameters with most of the accuracy of full fine-tuning and none of the forgetting risk. ##### Key takeaways - Early layers learn general features and late layers learn task-specific ones, which is why pretrained models transfer — you almost never train from scratch. - Choose feature extraction for small datasets and full fine-tuning for larger ones, adjusting for how far your domain sits from the pretraining data. - Use a learning rate around 2e-5 and 2–4 epochs; this single setting is the main defence against destroying pretrained knowledge. - Match the pretraining preprocessing exactly — the same tokenizer, the same image normalization statistics — or every layer receives an unexpected input distribution. - Progressive unfreezing and discriminative learning rates protect the backbone from a noisy new head, and LoRA gives you most of fine-tuning's benefit while training about 1% of the parameters.
